body:
{
  "hypotheses": [
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H1",
      "hypothesis": "Subject-level variation in wearable stress-detection uncertainty stems from individual differences in baseline autonomic tone, such as resting heart‑rate variability, which alters the mapping between physiological signals and stress labels.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Higher resting parasympathetic tone yields weaker stress‑evoked signal changes, increasing model uncertainty for those individuals.",
      "core_assumption": "Baseline autonomic tone is stable enough across measurement sessions to act as a subject‑specific modifier of stress‑related signal dynamics.",
      "knowledge_gap_addressed": "Limited understanding of how inter‑individual baseline autonomic states contribute to uncertainty in wearable stress detection.",
      "status": "SPECULATIVE"
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H2",
      "hypothesis": "Variability in skin impedance and epidermal properties across participants leads to heterogeneous PPG signal quality, thereby influencing uncertainty estimates.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Higher skin impedance attenuates PPG amplitude and increases noise, reducing signal‑to‑noise ratio and raising prediction uncertainty.",
      "core_assumption": "Skin impedance varies significantly between individuals and is not fully corrected by standard preprocessing pipelines.",
      "knowledge_gap_addressed": "Gap in quantifying how subject‑specific skin characteristics affect sensor‑derived stress signal reliability.",
      "status": "SPECULATIVE"
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H3",
      "hypothesis": "Circadian phase differences cause time‑of‑day‑dependent modulation of stress‑related physiology, producing subject‑specific uncertainty when models ignore temporal context.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Stress biomarkers exhibit circadian rhythms; misalignment between measurement time and a subject’s internal phase yields weaker or stronger signal changes, affecting confidence.",
      "core_assumption": "Each individual has a stable circadian phase that can be approximated by sleep/wake times or melatonin onset.",
      "knowledge_gap_addressed": "Lack of models that incorporate individual circadian timing to explain uncertainty in stress detection.",
      "status": "SPECULATIVE"
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H4",
      "hypothesis": "Inconsistent self‑report labeling of stress across participants introduces label noise that propagates to higher model uncertainty for certain subjects.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Subjects differ in interpretive bias, recall accuracy, and willingness to report stress, leading to heterogeneous ground‑truth quality.",
      "core_assumption": "Label noise is primarily driven by subject‑specific reporting tendencies rather than random error.",
      "knowledge_gap_addressed": "Unclear extent to which subject‑level labeling variability contributes to uncertainty estimates in wearable stress models.",
      "status": "SPECULATIVE"
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H5",
      "hypothesis": "Variability in sensor placement tightness and orientation across individuals creates differential motion artifact susceptibility, affecting uncertainty.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Looser coupling increases motion‑induced noise, degrading signal fidelity and raising prediction uncertainty for those users.",
      "core_assumption": "Placement tightness varies systematically between users and is not fully mitigated by algorithmic motion correction.",
      "knowledge_gap_addressed": "Insufficient knowledge of how subject‑specific wearing habits influence sensor‑derived stress signal reliability.",
      "status": "SPECULATIVE"
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H6",
      "hypothesis": "Genetic polymorphisms in catecholamine metabolism (e.g., COMT Val158Met) modulate the magnitude of physiological stress responses, leading to subject‑level uncertainty differences.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Variants causing higher enzymatic activity produce faster catecholamine clearance, blunting physiological stress signals and increasing model uncertainty.",
      "core_assumption": "Genotype‑dependent differences in stress‑reactivity are sufficiently large to be detectable via wearable signals.",
      "knowledge_gap_addressed": "Gap in linking genetic variation to observable differences in wearable stress‑signal uncertainty.",
      "status": "SPECULATIVE"
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H7",
      "hypothesis": "Within‑subject temporal non‑stationarity (habituation or sensitization to stressors) over weeks causes drift in the stress‑signal relationship, raising uncertainty for later measurements.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Repeated exposure alters physiological responsiveness, making earlier‑trained models less accurate and increasing uncertainty over time.",
      "core_assumption": "Stress‑response dynamics change measurably across longitudinal sessions for many individuals.",
      "knowledge_gap_addressed": "Limited understanding of how longitudinal physiological adaptation contributes to uncertainty in wearable stress detection.",
      "status": "SPECULATIVE"
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H8",
      "hypothesis": "Failure to stratify by activity context (e.g., exercise vs. sedentary) yields context‑dependent uncertainty that varies across subjects based on their typical activity patterns.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Physical activity induces overlapping physiological changes with stress, confounding signal interpretation; subjects with higher activity exposure exhibit greater uncertainty when context is ignored.",
      "core_assumption": "Activity‑induced physiological confounds are not fully captured by generic stress models.",
      "knowledge_gap_addressed": "Gap in quantifying how subject‑specific activity profiles affect uncertainty in stress detection when context is omitted.",
      "status": "SPECULATIVE"
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H9",
      "hypothesis": "Low per‑subject sample size leads to high variance in estimated model parameters (e.g., weights in a personalized classifier), directly increasing uncertainty estimates for those individuals.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Sparse data per user yields unstable parameter estimates, causing wider confidence intervals in predictions.",
      "core_assumption": "Parameter uncertainty scales inversely with the number of labeled samples available per subject.",
      "knowledge_gap_addressed": "Insufficient insight into how limited individual data contributes to uncertainty in wearable stress models.",
      "status": "SPECULATIVE"
    },
    {
      "hypothesis_id": "H10",
      "hypothesis": "Differences in sensor sampling rates and synchronization errors across devices introduce temporal misalignment that affects feature extraction, leading to subject‑specific uncertainty.",
      "proposed_mechanism": "Misaligned timestamps cause phase shifts in multimodal features (e.g., PPG vs. accelerometry), degrading model confidence for users with larger synchronization drift.",
      "core_assumption": "Sampling rate jitter and synchronization offsets vary between devices and are not fully corrected by standard interpolation.",
      "knowledge_gap_addressed": "Lack of knowledge on how subject‑level sensor timing inconsistencies propagate into uncertainty in stress detection.",
      "status": "SPECULATIVE"
    }
  ]
